You've told ChatGPT about your clients, your salary and your health. Deleting the chat doesn't delete what it remembered.

Here's how to see what ChatGPT and Claude kept about you, and lock it down in 5 minutes. Save this, then send it to the person on your team who pastes everything into AI.

ChatGPT
→ Settings → Data Controls → turn off "Improve the model for everyone." Your chats stop going into training
→ Settings → Personalization → Manage Memories. Delete one by one or all at once
→ Deleting a chat does NOT remove memories already saved from it
→ For anything sensitive, use Temporary Chat: deleted within 30 days, never used for training

Claude
→ Settings → Privacy → turn off "Model Improvement." With it on, chats can be kept for up to 5 years
→ A thumbs up or down stores the whole conversation for 5 years. Don't rate chats with client data
→ Incognito chats are never used for training
→ Deleted chats are wiped from Anthropic's servers within 30 days

Audit prompt (paste into ChatGPT with memory on):

"List everything you know or remember about me from saved memories and past chats. Group it by category: identity, work and clients, money, health, family, location, logins or keys. Mark anything sensitive, and tell me exactly which items I should delete and where."

Run it once. You'll see what you've been handing over.

Have you ever checked what your AI remembers about you, or are you scared to look?
@godofprompt Good reminder. I tell teams to treat these chats like email and assume anything you paste sticks around.

@godofprompt Good reminder. My rule before pasting anything into AI is to strip account numbers, addresses, PINs and SSNs first, so there's nothing sensitive to remember. I'd also skim the memory page now and then, the way you'd skim a bank statement.

text:
Ethan Mollick got a 3:41 movie out of Claude Opus 5.5 with two prompts. The second one was 18 words and ended with "figure it out."

Prompt 1: "Give me 10 brilliant ideas for a science fiction short short story, pick the most brilliant and execute it terribly"
Prompt 2: "Opus, great, now turn that into a movie, i know you can make it amazing. figure it out."

3 moves worth stealing:
→ Ask for 10, make it pick 1. The model throws out its own weak drafts before you see them
→ Give it a strange target. "Execute it terribly" set a clear style, and "make it good" never does
→ Once the context exists, delegate. Prompt 2 needed no spec because the story was the spec

Your first message carries the context. Every message after it can be short.

5 prompts built on the same moves:

Content: "Give me 10 post ideas for [audience] about [topic]. Pick the one most likely to get saved, explain why in one line, then write it in the voice of [specific person]."

Landing page: "Write 10 headlines for this page: [paste]. Pick the one a skeptical buyer would click, say why, then give 3 variations under 8 words."

Cold email: "Give me 10 opening lines for a cold email to [role]. Pick the one that sounds least like sales, then write the full email under 90 words."

Bad first: "Write the worst possible version of [X], full of every cliché. List the clichés you used. Now write the real version with none of them."

Follow-up: "Great. Now turn that into [format]. Figure it out."

What's the shortest prompt that ever gave you something great?

Ethan Mollick's post with the full movie: https://x.com/emollick/status/2117503772398178763

You pay $200 a month for Claude Max. The fastest way to lose it is a "free" agent that runs on your plan.

Three of them went viral this week. One tells you to share your plan with your whole team.

3 signs a tool will get your Claude account banned:

Sign 1: It asks you to paste a token or session cookie.
Anthropic's docs: developers may not "collect, store, or intermediate http://Claude.ai credentials or session tokens"

Sign 2: It says "share with your team."
Consumer Terms: you "may not make your Account available to anyone else"

Sign 3: It promises "unlimited."
Pro and Max limits "assume ordinary, individual usage." Unlimited usage on a capped plan is a magic trick, and your account is the rabbit.

This is already enforced:
→ February: OpenCode pulled Claude Pro and Max login after legal requests from Anthropic
→ April 4: Anthropic cut OpenClaw off subscription limits
→ Accounts were banned for running plans through third-party harnesses

Safe: Claude Code signed in with your own plan, http://Claude.ai, or any agent on your own API key.

Check any tool in 2 minutes:
"Here's an AI tool's landing page and docs: [paste]. Here are Anthropic's rules: [paste 'Authentication and credential use' from the Claude Code docs]. Tell me how it connects to Claude, whether it uses my plan or an API key, quote any line that breaks the rules, and give a verdict: safe, gray zone, or ban risk."

Would you risk your Max plan for unlimited agent runs, or keep agents on a separate API key?

Sources:
Claude Code docs, "Authentication and credential use": https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance
Anthropic Consumer Terms: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms

quoted_tweet.text:
Friday was my last day at Anthropic.

Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.

When we first launched, most people approved every permission prompt by hand and mostly used Claude to answer questions and write tests. 

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

Excited to see what you all make next!
